title: Architecture and Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-serving, Observability, Performance + ADR Index
author: Ava Chen
content:
Summary

This document collects Redwood Inference's cross-cutting architecture and engineering standards: API standards, coding standards, infrastructure (IaC) expectations, model-serving requirements, observability conventions, and performance SLOs. It also indexes the canonical ADRs (architecture decision records) that inform these standards and includes practical runbook-level guidance for teams implementing or onboarding services. This is the canonical reference for engineers, architects, and reviewers.

Purpose and scope

- Purpose: Provide a single, actionable set of standards to increase consistency, reliability, and operability across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Scope: Applies to all services and repos owned by engineering teams that ship production-facing inference, control-plane, or customer-facing APIs. Includes Redwood API, Dedicated control plane components, and Private deployment packages.

Principles (short)

1. Observable by default: Every service must emit metrics, structured logs, and traces.
2. Production-first ergonomics: defaults and templates should enforce safe defaults for SLOs, rate limits, and secrets handling.
3. Explicit compatibility and versioning for models and APIs.
4. Minimize blast radius: canary rollouts, circuit breakers, and multi-tier fallbacks.
5. Measurable cost/performance tradeoffs; document when choosing lower cost options (quantization, batching) and track regressions.

Section 1 — API standards

Overview
The Redwood API is a developer-facing REST/JSON interface for generation, chat, embeddings, and metadata operations. Internal control-plane APIs follow the same conventions unless otherwise noted. These standards are enforced by the API Gatekeeper review checklist.

1. URL and resource design
- Use plural nouns: /v1/models, /v1/inferences, /v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/usage.
- Use hierarchical routes for ownership and scoping.
- Avoid verbs in resource names; use action endpoints sparingly (POST /v1/models/{id}:deploy only when action semantics are required).

2. Versioning
- Base path versioning: /v1, /v2. Back-compatibility within a major version is required.
- Deprecation: Communicate 90-day minimum deprecation window for breaking changes, with automatic redirects and metrics on deprecated call usage.

3. Request/response format
- JSON over HTTPS (TLS 1.2+). Use application/json; charset=utf-8.
- Standard response envelope for errors: {"error_code": "string", "message": "user-facing string", "internal_id": "uuid"}.
- Return stable schema with JSON Schema files in repo root, referenced from the API spec.

4. Pagination and filtering
- Cursor-based pagination preferred for list endpoints. Provide next_cursor token and total_count when feasible.

5. Rate limiting and throttling
- 429 responses MUST include Retry-After header (seconds).
- Per-route and per-API tier quotas configured via the API Gateway. Default free-tier quotas documented in product docs.

6. Error handling and idempotency
- Use idempotency keys for non-idempotent operations (Idempotency-Key header).
- Map HTTP status codes to semantics; 4xx client, 5xx server. Provide machine-readable error codes.

7. Security
- All endpoints require authentication via bearer tokens (short lived) or mTLS for internal/private endpoints.
- Sensitive fields must be redacted from logs and traces.

Section 2 — Coding standards and repo hygiene

Languages and style
- Primary backend languages: Go (API/control plane), Rust/C++ (runtime hot paths), Python (data infra and evals). Follow idiomatic style for each language.
- Enforce formatting and linting in CI: gofmt/golangci-lint, rustfmt/clippy, black/flake8.

Testing and quality gates
- Unit tests required for all public functions and critical code paths. Target 80% coverage for new modules; measure coverage by package.
- Integration tests for service boundaries (mock network and end-to-end where feasible).
- Regression/e2e smoke test that runs against canary environments pre-rollout.

Code review and ownership
- All PRs require at least one approving review from an owner listed in OWNERS file. Large changes (>= 300 LOC) should have two reviewers from different squads.
- PR checklist: design rationale, backward compatibility notes, perf impact, observability additions, security implications.

Dependency management
- Use dependency scanning in CI (Snyk/OSS-catalog). Pin major versions and document upgrade plans in ADRs.

Secrets and keys
- No secrets in code or repo. Use Secrets Manager (AWS Secrets Manager / Vault). Pull secrets at runtime with short-lived credentials.

Section 3 — Infrastructure and IaC standards

IaC and provisioning
- All cloud resources must be declared in IaC (Terraform preferred). Avoid manual console changes; any exception requires a documented migration plan.
- Terraform modules: use company-standard modules in git::ssh://.../infra-modules.

Accounts, networking, and multitenancy
- Each environment (prod, staging, canary) has separate accounts/projects. Use VPCs with private subnets for runtime GPUs.
- Use service-per-VPC pattern for private customer deployments. Network ACLs, security groups, and private link endpoints required for sensitive services.

Capacity and GPU fleet standards
- Capacity manifests for Dedicated pools must include target utilization (target 65-75% avg), headroom(20% spare), and scaling policies. See GPU fleet runbook for thresholds.

Backups and DR
- Control-plane state required to be backed up daily with point-in-time recovery windows documented. RPO <= 1 hour for critical metadata; RTO targets documented per-service.

Section 4 — Model-serving standards

Packaging and model artifacts
- Model artifacts must be stored in immutable object storage with content-addressed names (sha256). Provide manifest.json with model: name, version, architecture, tokenizer, supported-sequence-length, quantization-profile.

Versioning and compatibility
- Semantic model versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Breaking changes increment MAJOR. Runtime must check manifest for compatibility and reject unsupported artifacts.

Quantization and profiles
- Quantization profiles must be named and documented (e.g., fp16, int8-tn8, int8-llm). Each profile includes accuracy impact summary (delta in evals) and recommended workloads.

Runtime lifecycle and KV cache
- Provide warmup hooks for large models (prefetch KV caches) and ensure lazy-load paths degrade gracefully. KV cache eviction policies should be documented per service.

Rollouts and fallbacks
- Canary policy: default 1% traffic for 24 hours, then 10% for 24 hours, then 100% if no regressions. All rollouts require an eval checklist and automatic rollback thresholds.
- Fallbacks: configure compatible lightweight model variants (smaller quantized model) with automated routing when latency SLO or capacity constraints are breached.

Operational controls
- Expose per-model metrics: tokens-served, avg_token_latency, p95_token_latency, errors_per_1M_tokens, memory_pressure.

Section 5 — Observability standards

Metrics
- Emit metrics in Prometheus format with stable metric names and labels. Use prefix rwinf_. Provide metrics for request lifecycle, model runtime internals, GPU utilization, queue length, and batching stats.
- SLO metrics: availability, latency percentiles, and error budget burn rate.

Logs
- Structured JSON logs with fields: timestamp, level, service, component, trace_id, span_id, request_id, tenant_id (if applicable), message, error_code. PII must not be logged.

Tracing
- Use OpenTelemetry for distributed tracing. Capture request_id and model-request-id for cross-service correlation. Sample rate default 1% in prod; increase for canary.

Dashboards and alerts
- Standard dashboard template for service health: availability, p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, request rate, CPU/GPU/Memory.
- Alerting thresholds (examples):
  - High error rate: error_rate > 0.5% for 5m -> page SRE.
  - Latency SLO burn: p95_latency > 2x target for 10m -> page oncall.
  - GPU memory OOM frequency: OOM_count > 1 in 1h -> page infra-team.

Incident instrumentation
- Each service must include debug endpoints: /health, /ready, /debug/heap, /debug/threads (restricted by auth). Post-incident, add missing telemetry as part of the remediation plan.

Section 6 — Performance standards and benchmarking

SLO definitions (platform-wide defaults)
- Availability: 99.9% per month for user-facing APIs.
- Inference latency (text gen): p50 < 120ms, p95 < 350ms, p99 < 900ms for baseline models under normal load on hosted fleet.
- Embeddings: p95 < 150ms.
- Throughput: documented per instance type in the model profile.

Benchmarking process
- Benchmark harness: use the benchmarking-and-perf-suite in eng-serving-runtime. Run representative workloads (token length distributions, concurrent clients) and produce a benchmark report with hardware, kernel selection, batching settings, and measured cost/token.
- Regression gate: any perf regression >10% for p95 or cost/token must be triaged in regression-triage and approved by performance owner.

Cost-performance controls
- Default serving profiles should include batching window, max batch size, KV cache warmup, and quantization suggestions. Document expected cost/token and accuracy delta in the model profile.

Section 7 — ADR index (decision records)

This section lists key ADRs that influenced the above standards. For full ADR content, see the ADRs folder in architecture-and-standards. Each ADR below includes a short summary and owners.

1) ADR-2025-01: Runtime kernel selection policy
- Decision: Use dynamic kernel selection based on model architecture and sequence-length distribution with a fallback to a conservative kernel when unknown.
- Rationale: Maximizes throughput for common workloads while reducing regressions on tails.
- Owner: Runtime team (owner: Rahul Singh).

2) ADR-2025-04: API versioning strategy
- Decision: Base path versioning (v1/v2) with compatibility guarantees within major versions.
- Owner: API Platform (owner: Leila Gomez).

3) ADR-2025-09: Default SLOs and alert thresholds
- Decision: Standardize on 99.9% availability and the latency percentiles listed above for client-facing APIs.
- Owner: SRE/Platform (owner: Marcus Reed).

How to add an ADR

1. Create a new ADR markdown file in architecture-and-standards/decision-records named ADR-YYYY-NN-title.md.
2. Include: status, date, context, decision, consequences, and owners.
3. PR must reference impacted services and update this index with a 1-2 sentence summary.

Operational checklist for new services

1. API design review (Gatekeeper) completed.
2. IaC module and environment provisioning in Terraform.
3. Metrics, logs, and tracing integrated with templates.
4. Canary rollout plan created with automatic rollback thresholds.
5. Benchmark report attached to PR showing cost/token and latency.

6. Security review for data residency and KMS integration if required.

Owners and escalation

- Architecture guardrails: eng-platform@redwood.com
- Runtime performance: eng-serving-runtime@redwood.com
- API Policy and Gatekeeper: eng-developer-experience@redwood.com
- SRE/incident: eng-sre@redwood.com

Appendix: Example configuration table for model profile

| key | example value | notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| model_name | rw-alpha-1 | canonical model id |
| version | 1.2.0 | semantic version |
| seq_len | 2048 | max supported sequence length |
| quant_profile | int8-tn8 | referenced quantization profile |
| warmup_tokens | 1024 | tokens to prepopulate KV cache |
| target_p95_ms | 350 | performance target for hosted fleet |
| cost_token_usd | 0.0004 | expected cost per token |

Contact and feedback

For questions or requests to relax a standard for a specific case, open an RFC in the architecture-and-standards board and tag the relevant owners. This doc is owned by eng-platform; periodic reviews are scheduled annually or after major infra/runtime changes.
